VaDar: Implicit Goal Conditioning
via Value Disaggregation

Shashwat Saxena 1,* Mehul Goel 1,* Sreyas Venkataraman 1,* Sarvesh Patil 1 Max Simchowitz 1,2

1 Carnegie Mellon University · 2 Amazon Scholar, Amazon FAR

* Equal contribution

Download Paper Explore the method ↓ BibTeX

VaDar trains a shared critic to predict returns at multiple temporal resolutions, from intermediate subgoals to final-task success. These values guide a single policy that requires no subgoal information at deployment.

01 / Subgoal myopia

Myopic subgoal completion can compromise future subtasks.

The ArrangeTea task in the RoboCasa suite requires placing a kettle and a mug on a tray, then closing the cabinet. In the rollout above, the robot completes the kettle-placement subgoal but leaves too little room for the mug. When it tries to place the mug, the collision knocks the kettle off the counter.

The kettle-placement reward counts this placement as a success even though it obstructs the mug. A policy trained only to maximize the current-subgoal value has no incentive to leave room for the next step.

Implicit hierarchical goal conditioning trains a policy without a goal input, but still optimizes the value of the current subgoal. It therefore remains susceptible to the same myopic behavior.

VaDar trains the policy using future-subgoal values. An accurate mug-placement value can favor kettle placements that leave room on the tray. Learning that value, however, requires assigning credit to actions taken well before the mug-placement reward.

Subgoals from the Robomimic ToolHang task. Each target uses its own subgoal reward and next-state value.

Under sparse final-task rewards, temporal-difference updates propagate information about success backward through successive states. The critic must learn accurate next-state values before these targets can reliably supervise earlier state-action pairs.

Intermediate subgoals provide supervision at multiple temporal resolutions. A grasp can be completed before a placement, and both can precede full-task success. VaDar uses each replay transition to predict all of these subgoal returns, with a separate temporal-difference target for each prediction.

All of these predictions share a critic backbone. Features learned from intermediate targets can therefore also help predict final-task returns. We examine this proposed transfer in the implicit Bellman-backup section.

Each subgoal reward remains sparse. The supervision is dense across subgoals because every sampled transition contributes a loss for every subgoal value.

We examine the contribution of intermediate targets with Last-Q, which retains all-subgoal critic supervision but uses only the final-subgoal value for policy extraction.

03 / Using the values

Next-future weighting optimizes beyond the current subgoal.

ToolHang / animated training diagram

Select values for the policy update

Schematic, not rollout data
Critic supervision: all subgoals Policy extraction: selected values
1. Sample transition 2. Supervise all values 3. Apply weights 4. Update policy

The dots show training signals. Each stage illustrates a different task state; a policy update does not itself complete a subgoal.

The critic learns every subgoal value; the weighting scheme determines which values train the policy. Current-myopic uses only the first unfinished subgoal. Current-future includes that subgoal and all later ones. Our default, next-future, uses only the later values, except at the final subgoal, where it keeps the final value.

In ArrangeTea, current-myopic extraction can favor a kettle placement that obstructs the mug. Future-subgoal values account for the effect of that placement on subsequent task completion.

The animation follows the ToolHang task from the Robomimic suite. The robot must grasp a frame and insert it into a stand before grasping and hanging a wrench. During frame insertion, next-future uses the wrench-grasping and wrench-hanging values. Both later subgoals require the frame to stay inserted. The critic still learns the insertion value, although that value does not enter the policy update at this stage.

A future-subgoal value evaluates the current state and action, so the wrench-hanging value can favor a frame insertion needed for later success. Next-future weighting thus gives the policy a reason to complete the current subgoal without optimizing its value directly.

We apply the base algorithm's policy loss to the weighted sum, using OGPO, FQL, or SAC. Subgoal information determines the weights during training. The deployed policy takes only the state, with no subgoal selector or completion labels.

Critic update and completed subgoals

For each replay transition, we compute a reward and temporal-difference target for every subgoal, then sum the critic losses. VaDar clips the targets to cap values for completed subgoals, whose completion reward would otherwise accumulate. See the paper for the clipping rule and the extension from sequential subgoals to a directed acyclic graph.

04 / Results

VaDar improves learning on long-horizon manipulation tasks.

View successful rollouts

We begin with behavior-cloned policies that have low success rates, then fine-tune them with reinforcement learning. Within each comparison, all methods use the same base algorithm for policy extraction. The baselines include hierarchical and implicit hierarchical goal conditioning, dense preference rewards, and the sparse-reward base algorithm.

With OGPO on RoboCasa, VaDar is the only method in this comparison to converge on LoadDishwasher. On PreSoakPan, it reaches nearly twice the success rate of the strongest baseline, implicit hierarchical goal conditioning.

The benefit varies across tasks and algorithms. On Robomimic, VaDar performs similarly to goal-conditioned methods with OGPO, but learns faster on Transport and ToolHang with FQL. On OGBench with SAC, it performs comparably to the goal-conditioned baselines. In all of these settings, VaDar deploys a policy that does not need goal information.

05 / Understanding the gains

Intermediate supervision improves final-task critic learning.

To isolate the contribution of critic supervision, we train Last-Q with targets for every subgoal but use only the final-subgoal value to train its policy. Last-Q therefore has the same policy objective as the sparse-reward baseline; only its critic receives the extra intermediate targets.

Last-Q substantially outperforms the sparse-reward baseline on RoboCasa and approaches next-future VaDar on several tasks. The policy objective is unchanged, so the improvement supports the benefit of intermediate supervision for learning the final-task critic.

Future-aware policy extraction improves sample efficiency.

We then vary the policy weighting scheme while keeping all-subgoal critic supervision and the subgoal-independent policy architecture fixed. Current-myopic does not outperform the goal-conditioned baselines. Current-future and next-future improve sample efficiency and are the only variants in this comparison to converge on LoadDishwasher. Dense critic supervision alone is insufficient when policy extraction remains myopic.

Future-aware extraction also helps goal-conditioned policies on PreSoakPan with OGPO, bringing them close to VaDar. Removing the goal input alone therefore does not explain the gains.

Aggregating rewards does not recover the gains.

With exact values, a common policy, and fixed weights, aggregating values is equivalent to evaluating the aggregated reward. A neural critic need not learn the two equally well. VaDar also uses state-dependent weights and clipped targets, which fall outside this equivalence.

We compare against VaDar-Shaped, which aggregates subgoal rewards before the Bellman backup and trains a scalar critic. It fails to learn on the harder RoboCasa tasks and is less sample efficient elsewhere. Together with Last-Q, these results suggest that reward shaping alone does not explain the gains from all-subgoal critic supervision.

06 / Isolating critic quality

Test-time steering with a frozen policy.

We also isolate critic quality by holding a behavior-cloned policy fixed throughout training and evaluation. The critic learns to select among actions proposed by that policy.

Following Q-chunking , we sample candidate action chunks from the frozen policy and execute the one with the highest critic value. We train the VaDar critic and a Sparse critic, supervised only by final-task rewards, on the same demonstrations and frozen-policy rollouts. With four candidates, VaDar improves ArrangeTea success from 23% to 55% and ToolHang from 32% to 77%; the Sparse critic reaches 23% and 44%, respectively.

The improved action selection supports the benefit of subgoal supervision for critic learning independently of policy updates. This steering experiment uses subgoal-completion indicators at inference to compute next-future weights. The policies learned in the main experiments require no such indicators.

07 / Implicit Bellman backup

An implicit Bellman-backup view of dense critic supervision.

The steering experiment shows better action selection with a fixed policy, while Last-Q shows better learning when only the final-subgoal value trains the policy. We hypothesize that intermediate targets help by training shared features useful for predicting final-task returns.

With sparse final-task rewards, one-step TD learning propagates the reward signal backward through successive bootstrapped targets. For a fixed policy, the classical Bellman recursion is

A state far from task completion may already be close to an intermediate subgoal. Predicting this nearer outcome can train useful features before the final-task value is accurate. VaDar supervises every subgoal prediction at each transition, and their shared network parameters make these features available to the final-subgoal prediction.

We call this proposed transfer an implicit Bellman backup: learning from shorter-horizon targets may help the critic learn dependencies across stages of the task. Last-Q and frozen-policy steering support this interpretation, but do not establish extra Bellman backups within a forward pass or a guaranteed reduction in TD updates. See Section 6.4 of the paper for the full discussion.

08 / Multi-objective learning

Value disaggregation also supports multi-objective learning.

Separate values can also represent different objectives. In this PushT variant, the robot must align a T-shaped block with its target while avoiding a circular obstacle. It receives a sparse task reward and a dense penalty for proximity to the obstacle.

With a large penalty weight, a critic trained on the summed reward can struggle to learn successful pushing. We compare it with a critic that learns task completion and obstacle avoidance separately.

Separate critic targets for task completion and safety.

VaDar uses SAC with two critic heads, each trained against its own temporal-difference target. The policy uses their weighted sum:

These weights stay constant. The safety value predicts the return from the proximity penalty, and λ controls how much it influences the policy. Neither objective is a prerequisite for the other, so this experiment does not use next-future weighting.

Our comparison method, Agg-SAC, sums the same reward components and trains one scalar critic. We match the SAC backbone, network sizes, and training budget. Both methods are pretrained on the obstacle-free task, then fine-tuned for 800,000 environment steps.

VaDar is less sensitive to the safety weight.

Agg-SAC matches VaDar at small safety weights, but its success falls to nearly zero at λ = 5 or 10. VaDar continues to learn at these larger weights and fluctuates less during training across the sweep.

We conjecture that this improvement arises in part from the critic targets: each VaDar head fits a λ-independent target, while Agg-SAC incorporates λ into its target. VaDar applies the safety weight only when aggregating values for policy extraction.

09 / Scope and open questions

Extensions beyond sequential subgoals.

VaDar also supports subgoals arranged in a directed acyclic graph. The training labels need not come from simulator state: on the RoboCasa PreSoakPan task, a vision-language model supplies labels that yield similar final success to oracle labels, with a modest change in sample efficiency.

We still specify the subgoal structure in advance. Extending the method to continuous or combinatorially large goal spaces, including image- and language-described goals, remains open.
